events.title: Printed and painted silk gauze in a Han tomb at Mawangdui
events.summary: Tomb 1 at Mawangdui yielded a robe of printed and painted gauze. Search summaries of the Hunan Museum's and the Metropolitan Museum's pages say the Han printing was done with a stencil or stamp and then hand-coloured, which is not the same as printing with a carved block. This study has not been able to read either page (the Hunan Museum page timed out and the Met's site returned HTTP 429), so this entry is PENDING and makes no claim about how the cloth was printed.
events.significance: Printing on cloth in China is far older than printing on paper; the exact method at Mawangdui is still to be checked.

events.title: The Diamond Sutra: the oldest dated printed book
events.summary: A Buddhist text was carved onto woodblocks and printed as a long scroll, with the date 11 May 868. It is printed on paper, not cloth: the best-dated early product of block printing is a book, and this study found no source that settles whether printing on textiles came first.
events.significance: Shows the carved-block principle fully developed by the 9th century, in China.

events.title: A carved wooden textile printing block from Egypt
events.summary: The Met holds a carved wooden block catalogued as a textile printing block of the 10th century, from Egypt. It is the tool itself, not a print: a real carved block, a thousand years old.
events.significance: What a printing block looks like, and the earliest dated one in the Met's open collection.

events.title: Block-printed cottons from India found in Egypt
events.summary: At Quseir al-Qadim, a Red Sea port, 68 cotton fragments were found that match the 'Fustat' textiles identified as Gujarati: resist- and mordant-dyed cottons, mostly block-printed, dyed with indigotin and/or a red colorant from madder or morinda roots. The Quseir find was the first of its kind from a site excavated under datable conditions. Cleveland's catalogue dates a block-printed cotton fragment from Mamluk Egypt to the 1200s–1300s.
events.significance: The first secure datable proof that block-printed, mordant-dyed Indian cloth was traded across the Indian Ocean.

sources.institution: Ashmolean Museum, Eastern Art Online (Yousef Jameel Centre for Islamic and Asian Art)
sources.title: Indian textiles (Newberry collection essay)

They are resist- and mordant- dyed textiles, mostly block-printed.

events.title: A Gujarat cotton with trefoils, found in Cairo
events.place: Made in Gujarat (probably); found in Cairo
events.summary: The V&A's fragment IS.73-1972 is printed, mordant and resist-dyed cotton, made in India (Gujarat, probably) in the 15th century and found in Cairo. Its pattern 'consists of geometrical shapes, each filled with a variety of smaller patterns including trefoils', in red and white on an indigo ground.
events.significance: Trefoils, madder red and indigo on one printed cotton: the closest later echo of the Priest-King's motif that this study has found. A resemblance across 3,000 years is not a lineage.

events.title: A carved printing block from India
events.summary: The Met's carved wooden printing block from India, 15th–16th century, shows the tool behind the Gujarati cottons that reached Egypt. The Met records it only as 'India', so the marker on the map is approximate.
events.significance: The Indian side of the same tradition as the Egyptian block, in wood, carved.

events.title: Block printing reaches Europe, late
events.summary: The V&A: block printing of textiles 'seems to have come to Europe comparatively late, as there is no evidence that it was practised there earlier than the 14th century'. It may have been introduced into Italy first, then spread into Germany. The museum also notes that little is known about printing or the makers of printed textiles in the 14th century. The marker is approximate.
events.significance: Europe learned block printing about a thousand years after the Indian Ocean and China had it, which is why the Asian imports of the 17th century were such a shock.

events.title: Indian imports start European calico printing
events.summary: A V&A printed calico of 1690–1700, probably made in England or the Netherlands, comes with this account: Indian painted textiles imported by the Dutch, English and French East India Companies gave a direct incentive to make satisfactory substitutes at home, and this led to the development of European calico printing industries. Giorgio Riello adds that Europeans found it hard to replicate mordant-based printing and dyeing.
events.significance: The moment the craft this site follows crosses into industry.

sources.title: Printed cotton, calico (12-1884)
sources.quote: Quantities of Indian painted textiles were imported into Europe by the Dutch, English and French East India Companies during the 17th century. They provided a direct incentive for the production of satisfactory substitutes at home, and this led to the development of European calico printing industries.

sources.institution: London School of Economics, Global Economic History Network (working paper by Giorgio Riello)
sources.title: The Rise of Calico Printing in Europe and the Influence of Asia in the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries
sources.quote: For many decades, Europeans were unable to produce pure cotton cloth and had great difficulty in replicating mordant-based textile printing and dyeing.

events.title: France lifts its ban on printed cottons
events.summary: Riello writes that calico printing spread from Basle to Mulhouse and Neuchâtel and 'from there back to France after the ban was lifted in 1759'. This study did not find the 1686 French ban's own text, so the start of the prohibition is not stated here.
events.significance: Prohibitions, not demand, set the pace of European calico printing.

events.title: A printshop at Jouy-en-Josas
events.summary: Riello cites a printed vignette of a printshop in Jouy-en-Josas belonging to the calico printer Oberkampf in the early 1780s. The Met holds the printed cloth 'Les Travaux de la Manufacture', dated 1783: a textile that shows the works that made it.
events.significance: A rare picture of block printing at work, printed on the cloth.

events.title: Stamped adinkra cloth reaches the British Museum
events.summary: A British Art Studies article describes adinkra as a stamped textile, made of cotton woven in long strips and decorated with repeated patterns in a grid. Thomas Bowdich acquired objects including stamped adinkra cloth on an 1816–18 mission centred on an 1817 journey to Kumase, and presented them to the British Museum in 1818 (formally added in 1831).
events.significance: Block-style stamping developed independently of the Indian and Chinese traditions, in West Africa.

events.title: Morris revives indigo discharge and the hand block
events.summary: William Morris designed 'Strawberry Thief' in 1883 (V&A) and printed it with the indigo discharge method, 'an ancient technique used for many centuries mostly in Asia'. Cleveland's record says the process required the entire cloth to be dyed blue before it was bleached and block printed.
events.significance: Block printing survives industrialisation as a deliberate craft, borrowing from Asia.
